title: Sukkot: the booth
hookLine: a flimsy hut with a leafy roof, where people eat for a week under the stars

cards: Every fall, on certain streets, they appear: little huts on balconies, in backyards, in parking lots, even on apartment rooftops. Walls of canvas or plywood.
A roof of palm fronds, bamboo mats or branches, with gaps you can see through. Paper chains and hanging fruit. A folding table inside, and a family eating dinner in their coats.
Some even sleep out there. There's a custom of starting to build the night Yom Kippur ends, still tasting the first meal after the fast. For a week, the fanciest room in the house is a shack.

teach.b: The hut is a sukkah, and the holiday is Sukkot, the plural: booths. It begins on the fifteenth of the seventh month, under the full moon, and lasts seven days.
The Torah says: "Ye shall dwell in booths seven days," so each generation would remember that the Israelites lived in booths when they came out of Egypt.
It's also a harvest festival, the last gathering of the year before the rains, and the Torah calls it a time to rejoice. The rabbis call it the season of our joy.
The Talmud sets the minimum at two full walls and part of a third. It has to be temporary.

teach.h: A ROOF YOU CAN SEE STARS THROUGH.
teach.b: And the roof must be things that grew from the ground and have been cut, like branches or reeds, thick enough for more shade than sun by day, and ideally loose enough to see the stars at night.
So right after Yom Kippur, people move out of solid homes into something fragile. Why?
The Talmud records two views of the booths in the wilderness: one rabbi says they were real huts, another says they were clouds of glory, God's protection overhead.
Either way, a roof of branches becomes a way to remember being sheltered.

teach.h: GUESTS, AND GO IN IF IT RAINS.
teach.b: There are guests too. Each night, some families welcome ushpizin: Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Moses, Aaron, Joseph and David, and in some homes the women of the Bible as well, and real guests share the meal.

teach.h: YE SHALL DWELL IN BOOTHS SEVEN DAYS.
teach.b: And if it pours? The Mishnah says go inside. The sukkah is for joy, not misery.

how: During Sukkot, many Jewish families build a sukkah with a roof of cut branches or reeds and eat their meals in it for seven days, some sleeping there too. Some welcome the ushpizin, biblical guests, along with real ones.

games.why: the Mishnah says that when the rain would spoil the food, go inside: the sukkah is for joy, not misery.

practice: Picture a meal outside, on a porch, a park bench or a step, under a roof of loose branches with the sky showing through.

Think about what in your life is sturdier than it looks and what's more fragile than it looks, a job, a body, a friendship, and hold both kinds lightly. If you pray, you might give thanks for shelter.

wordCard.voice: Sukkah. A booth: a temporary hut with a roof of branches, where Jews eat, and some sleep, for the seven days of Sukkot.

orig.note: Hebrew: a booth, a hut; the festival is Sukkot, booths.

carryVoice: Your line: live lightly for a week. A good meal needs less than you'd think. That's day one hundred twenty-seven.
